accounts.html: An account in Daimond is a passphrase held on this device. There is no account on a server: your identity, your keys and your files live only in this browser. This page covers the passphrase, sharing a browser with other people, and what stays private.
On first run Daimond offers to

. You give a name and a passphrase, and that passphrase becomes your account. It does two jobs: it encrypts your stored provider key and mail credentials so an onlooker cannot read them, and it is the identity that signs you in for credits. Nothing about it leaves the browser.
The passphrase is never stored and cannot be recovered.

Daimond keeps only the encrypted data, not the passphrase that unlocks it. If you forget it, the encrypted keys and credentials are gone — so keep it somewhere safe. You can carry on without one by choosing
, but a provider key is best added once a passphrase is protecting it.
A faster unlock with a passkey
Once a passphrase is protecting the app, you can add a

for a faster unlock: a face, a fingerprint, or a security key, the same passwordless sign-in your device already offers. A passkey does not replace the passphrase, it unseals it for you, so the passphrase stays the root and the always-available fallback, and a lost passkey costs you nothing as long as you still hold the passphrase. None of this reaches a server: the unlock happens entirely on the device, and the credits service only ever sees a public key.
Your identity sits at the top of the admin panel, bottom-left. The admin home lists the controls for it:
The account controls in the admin panel: change name, change passphrase, export or import a backup, log out, and forget this identity.
The account controls: change your name or passphrase, back up or restore, log out, or forget the identity entirely.

More than one person on one browser
Daimond holds one account at a time in a browser, so sharing a computer is a matter of locking and, if needed, replacing:
to lock the app. Your chats, keys and files remain on the device but cannot be read without your passphrase, so the next person cannot see your work.
Enter your passphrase to unlock and pick up exactly where you left off.
Handing the browser to someone else for good.

Because there is no server, your account does not follow you automatically. To use it on another browser or machine,
Anyone who imports it becomes you, so treat the backup file like the passphrase itself — keep it private and do not send it over a channel you would not trust with the passphrase.

Your passphrase, provider keys, mail credentials, chats, Diamonds and files live in this browser and are not sent to us. What we hold on the gateway is money and ciphertext: your credit balance and licences, and, for cross-device sync, one encrypted parcel we cannot open. We do not have the key, so we cannot read your work.

It helps to know exactly where data goes. Your messages go to a model provider when you connect your own key, or through our metered service when you spend credits on a model. Fetching a web page to read, and syncing or sending mail, pass through the gateway to reach the outside world. And a sync carries an encrypted parcel between your own devices. So the honest claim is not that nothing ever leaves, but this: with your own key, your chats and files never leave in the clear, and you can watch only ciphertext leave for our servers.
You need not take that on trust.

Daimond's client — the code that runs in this browser and decides what is sent — is open source. You can read it, build it, and open your browser's network panel to confirm for yourself that only ciphertext leaves. The one claim every private tool makes, we let you check: the source is at

The protection has honest limits. The passphrase guards against casual local inspection and shared-device snooping — someone who opens the browser's developer tools finds only encrypted data, not your keys. It does not protect against a compromised browser, a malicious extension, or a keylogger watching the passphrase as you type it. Those defeat any in-browser scheme and are out of scope, so keep the device itself trustworthy. And what a remote server does inside itself, ours or anyone's, cannot be proven from the outside: the few operations that pass through the gateway rest on that openness and on our stated policy, which is exactly why it is the client, the part you can check, that we open to you.
Daimond runs in your browser. Nothing here is sent to us.

A Diamond is a durable container for a pursuit — where what you have worked out about a piece of work is kept, so that later work starts from it. This page covers starting and reading chats, the turn controls, folding a chat into a Diamond, and organising the Diamonds you accumulate.

Folding a chat into a Diamond
When a conversation has worked something out, you fold it: you keep what you learnt and drop the back-and-forth that produced it. What you fold into is a
Two units make up a Diamond:
is one improvement — a single step forward.

You fold a step you have

Nothing is absorbed on its own.

A crystal never grows in the background: you choose the turns that are offered, and the fold itself is a proposal — the agent rewrites the crystal and shows you the result, which you accept or reject. A crystal only changes because you said so.
The Diamond command surface shown in place of the chat, with controls to steer and fold the method.
Selecting a Diamond shows its command surface in place of the chat, where you steer and fold the method.
Diamonds are listed above your chats in the rail; add one with the

. Selecting a Diamond replaces the chat in the centre with its command surface — a compact view where you steer the work and fold further improvements into it. You can tell which face the panel is showing without reading it: on a Diamond the panel takes the Daimond mark beside the name and squares its corners, against the rounded corners of everything else on screen. The conversation returns the moment you pick a chat again, because Daimond is built around the conversation and comes back to it whenever the stage would otherwise be empty.
What a Diamond does, and what it does not

A Diamond retains; it does not run. Nothing executes a crystal. There is no workflow engine behind a Diamond, nothing schedules it, nothing chains one Diamond to another, and there is no saved job waiting to fire. Returning to a Diamond does not set it going — and neither does leaving it alone, since a Diamond at rest stays exactly as you left it.

means you steer it again, with everything it has learnt already in hand. That is the whole of the claim, and it is worth more than it sounds. The crystal is prose, and prose is what a model reads best: it is handed to the daimon as context when you work the Diamond, and to every worker dispatched from it. What you worked out once reaches the work again without you retyping it — or remembering that you should.
The crystal is a real file —
, in the Diamond's own folder in your workspace. You can open it, read it, and edit it yourself, like any other file.
Every write to a crystal snapshots a version, so a crystal has a history and nothing is written over. The history lists every version, newest first, each with what produced it:
— see the raw input a fold consumed, the material the agent was given to reduce.
The text that was current is kept in the history first, so restoring an older version adds to the history rather than replacing it — a restore you did not mean can itself be undone.

A Diamond also keeps track of what its work touched: the files written and the pages opened while you were working on it. You do not have to record any of this. Daimond already notes every tool an agent uses, so the list is read off what happened — and it is gathered at the moment you accept a fold.

index.html: Daimond is an AI agent workspace that runs entirely in your browser. There is no account on a server and no app to install: your chats, keys and files live only on this device.

Nothing leaves your device unless you direct it to. Daimond reaches the outside world only at your request: when you connect your own model provider, so your messages go to that provider; when you spend credits to run a model, fetch a page, or sync mail; and when you link a second device. Everything else stays in this browser, and
sets out exactly what goes where, and how you can check it for yourself.

The history is not a separate changelog kept beside the app. It is the same published record Daimond's own delivery check reads: every build Daimond has ever served, in order, in a chain that cannot be rewritten without breaking. The one-line note on each entry was added without disturbing that chain, so what you are reading is annotated history rather than a retelling of it.
The planned entry looks different because it is different.

It carries no build id and no seal number, and says in words that it is not built yet and not promised for a date. Everything below it is sealed and checkable; a statement of intent is neither, and should not borrow the authority of a record.

There is no way back to an older build, and that is a choice rather than an omission. A pinned old build walks into the gateway's own refusal to talk to a client that is too old; it can hold a security fault that has since been fixed, which matters in an app holding your provider keys, your identity and your passkeys; and an old build meeting newer local data — your files, the durability journal, a sync parcel from another device — risks reading it wrong. Dislike of a change is answered at the change, by saying plainly what changed, which is what the notes in this history are for.

The stage is the middle zone. Its occupants take the stage on their own or two side by side, and never dock at the right. The point of two seats is that you never leave the conversation to do a thing: read the message, watch the page, read the document, with the daimon still beside it to be asked about it.

Keeping an arrangement with a Diamond

When a Diamond is selected, the appearance menu offers to keep the current arrangement of panels with it. Opening that Diamond again puts the arrangement back, so returning to a piece of work does not mean reassembling by hand the panels it needs. It is saved only when you ask — never inferred, and never in the background — because a switch that silently closed panels would read as work being lost. The menu also lets you update a saved arrangement, or forget it.

models.html: A daimon thinks with a model. You can bring your own provider key and pay that provider directly, or buy credits and let Daimond run a model for you. This page covers both, and how to keep credits topped up.
Two ways to power a daimon
Connect an account you already hold with a model provider. Your messages go straight to that provider; Daimond is not in the path, and nothing is charged by us.
No provider account to manage. Daimond runs the model for you and draws down the credits you bought. No subscription: you keep what you buy.
Either is enough to start. You can do both — connect a key for everyday work and keep credits for when you would rather not manage one.

Payment is handled on the payment provider's own hosted page. No card number, expiry or security code is ever typed into Daimond, so there is nothing here to leak.

Auto-reload is a standing instruction to buy your own credits when they run low, so a long job does not stop halfway. It is the one place Daimond is allowed to charge a saved card while you are away, so it is deliberately explicit. Three numbers set it, found below the packs in the Credits view:
— the balance at which a top-up fires.

— a hard cap on total top-ups in a calendar month. This is the number that matters: it is a ceiling, not a target, and it is enforced on the same code path as the charge, so it cannot be walked around.

Auto-reload cannot be switched on without a saved card — a control that turned on and then silently failed would be worse than one that is disabled and says why. Saving a card is a redirect to the payment provider's hosted page; Daimond never sees the card details.

A workspace that can run many agents at once can, in principle, spend fast. The danger is not a large monthly total — it is a

: a fan-out that burns through credit in seconds before you can react. Daimond is built to catch that spike, not merely to tally the total after the fact. Four measures work together, and none of them asks you to set a limit in advance.
A pace check before a fan-out runs.

The cost of dispatching a batch of agents is known before any of them starts. When a batch would run faster than your own recent pace, Daimond pauses it and asks you once, with the number and the estimate on the prompt. A few agents of ordinary cost never reach it; a sudden fifty do. The measure of “too fast” is your own normal, learned from your recent spend, so there is nothing to configure.
Pause and stop, always to hand.
panel lets you hold every running agent at a stroke, or stop them outright. Pausing stops the spend at once and keeps the work, so you lose nothing by pulling the brake to look.
A separate key for every agent.

Each agent running on credits spends its own freshly minted key, and each key is capped against what is genuinely left after its siblings' claims. Because no two agents ever share a key, parallel agents cannot race a shared allowance past its cap — a whole class of overspend simply cannot happen.
Everything metered, per turn, on your device.
Every model call is priced and recorded here as it happens, feeding the graphs above. The bill is never a surprise arriving later; it is in front of you as it is spent.
The intent is plain: run a team of agents without fear that a mistake — a runaway loop, a fan-out larger than you realised — can cost more than a glance and a click can undo.

sync.html: Daimond is local-first, so a second device starts empty. Cross-device sync carries your chats and workspace files between your own devices without the server ever reading them.

What travels through the gateway is one encrypted parcel that only your devices hold the key to. The key comes from your passphrase and never leaves the browser, so the server stores the parcel but cannot open it. Nothing readable crosses between devices.

Any file travels, whatever kind it is. A photograph, a recording, a PDF or a spreadsheet reaches your other devices as text does, up to a gigabyte for one file.

What syncs is also what is kept in cloud storage, so a workspace can be larger than the device you are reading it on. A file that is not on this device at the moment still shows in the tree, marked with a cloud, and comes down when you ask for it.
